items.q: How many distinct values can a single byte (8 bits) represent?

explain.right: Each bit has 2 states and there are 8 of them, so a byte has 2^8 = 256 possible patterns (values 0-255).
explain.wrong: 8 is the number of bits, not combinations; 64 and 1000 don't match any power of two for 8 bits.

items.q: Why is hexadecimal handy for reading bytes?
options: Hex can store more information than binary in the same space
One hex digit equals exactly 4 bits, so two hex digits represent one byte
Computers store data in hex rather than binary
Hex numbers are a completely different kind of number from binary

explain.right: Hex is base 16, and one hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits, so a byte (8 bits) is neatly two hex digits.
explain.wrong: Hex, binary, and decimal are just spellings of the same values; computers still store bits, and hex holds no more information than the bits it represents.

items.q: In the ASCII/Unicode world, how is the letter 'A' actually stored?
options: As a picture of the shape 'A'
As the literal letter A, which computers understand directly
As a number (code point) that a codebook maps to the character 'A'
As a special 'letter' type separate from numbers

explain.right: Text is numbers: a codebook like ASCII/Unicode assigns 'A' a number (65), and software maps it back to the character.
explain.wrong: Computers only store numbers/bits, not shapes or letters directly; there is no separate 'letter' storage beneath the bits.

items.q: In UTF-8, which statement is true?
options: Characters take 1 to 4 bytes, so one character is not always one byte
Every character always takes exactly two bytes
Bytes and characters are the same thing
Every character always takes exactly one byte

explain.right: UTF-8 is variable length: ASCII characters use 1 byte while others (accents, CJK, emoji) use 2-4, so character count can differ from byte count.
explain.wrong: Fixed one- or two-byte-per-character claims describe other schemes, not UTF-8; conflating bytes with characters is the classic encoding bug.

items.q: In one or two sentences, explain why the same photo can be described as 'just bits' and also as a meaningful image.
rubric: States the data is physically stored as bits (0s/1s), grouped into bytes
Notes that software/an agreed format interprets those bits as pixels/an image
Conveys that meaning comes from interpretation, not from the bits themselves

explain.right: Good answers say the file is literally bits, and a format/program agrees how to read those bits as pixels, so meaning is layered on by interpretation.
explain.wrong: A weak answer treats the image as inherently 'a picture' inside the computer, missing that bits only mean something via an agreed interpretation.
